implementation.name: SoftVelocity Clarion Data Dictionary and AppGen
implementation.version_scope: The publisher's graphical database-application workflow; licensed product editions and templates affect available features.

sources.label: Clarion database, dictionary and generated-application workflow
Clarion vendor licence and subscription categories

fit.text: Build business database applications with SQL or local ISAM data sources.

prerequisites.text: Start with the data schema and Data Dictionary; the wizard workflow introduces application generation without initial handwritten source.

execution.text: AppGen generates Clarion code from templates after the wizard captures the desired application behavior.

behavior.text: Dictionary definitions and selected templates determine the generated application's data and behavior.

tooling.text: The documented workflow centers on Data Dictionary, Wizards and AppGen, with support through the vendor's forums.

maintenance.text: Preserve dictionary and template choices when maintaining generated applications; the workflow depends on both.

costs.text: The vendor sells new licences, subscriptions, upgrades and add-ons; the appropriate product's current terms determine acquisition cost.

example.run_instructions: Use a licensed Clarion installation and its installed tutorial to define a small non-production database in Data Dictionary, then generate an application through Wizards/AppGen. The public vendor overview describes this graphical workflow but supplies no complete compilable textual example.
example.expected_result: A database application is generated from the chosen dictionary and templates; its screens depend on that selection.

implementation.name: Clean 3.1 system with clm
implementation.version_scope: Stable Clean 3.1 and its Unix-like command-line workflow; newer iTask packages use a separately documented package path.

sources.label: Clean language, iTask/mTask and Cloogle scope
Clean function declarations and Start evaluation
Clean clm/cpm command-line build instructions
Clean stable distributions and package distinctions
Clean 3.1 licence and library exclusions
SPDX BSD two-clause licence with views sentence

fit.text: Write pure, lazy functional programs; the project also documents iTask workflow and mTask embedded DSLs.

prerequisites.text: The introduction assumes programming basics; learn type signatures, pattern alternatives and the Start entry value.

execution.text: On Linux/macOS, clm compiles a main module and cpm manages projects; the installation guide describes environment setup.

behavior.text: Program execution computes Start; ordered pattern alternatives determine which matching function equation is used.

tooling.text: Cloogle searches libraries, syntax and compiler errors; Windows distributions include an IDE.

maintenance.text: Stable Clean 3.1 downloads and newer iTask packages have different distribution paths; select the matching documentation.

costs.text: The core distribution has BSD two-clause terms with a views disclaimer; Platform/Gast libraries and examples have separate licences.

example.code:
module Sum
import StdEnv
Start :: Int
Start = 2 + 4 + 6
example.run_instructions: After configuring the Clean command-line environment according to its Unix-like installation guide, run clm Sum -o sum and then ./sum.
example.expected_result: Evaluation of Start prints the integer 12.

licenses.scope: Clean 3.1 distribution except the explicitly excluded Platform/Gast libraries and examples.
licenses.notice: Retain copyright, conditions and disclaimer; review Platform/Gast directories and examples separately.

implementation.name: Clojure on the JVM with Clojure CLI
implementation.version_scope: The JVM implementation; language and CLI versions are selected separately through deps.edn.

sources.label: Clojure CLI execution and dependency selection
Clojure functional/JVM design
Clojure supported Java and platform installation paths
Clojure forms, REPL exploration and printing
Clojure Eclipse Public License 1.0

fit.text: Build functional Lisp programs that consume JVM libraries; persistent data structures and concurrency facilities shape the design.

prerequisites.text: Install Java and the CLI; learn nested forms and use an editor that supports evaluating them.

execution.text: The CLI constructs a JVM classpath and invokes a REPL, function or main/script entry according to its execution mode.

behavior.text: Prefix forms place the function before its arguments; println writes a human-readable value followed by a newline.

tooling.text: REPL documentation and source commands help explore functions; deps.edn controls project dependencies.

maintenance.text: The CLI can run independently selected Clojure language versions; record both versions for reproducible projects.

costs.text: Clojure uses EPL-1.0; the chosen Java distribution and application libraries have separate terms.

example.run_instructions: Install a supported Java runtime and the Clojure CLI, then run clojure -M sum.clj.

implementation.name: CoffeeScript 2 compiler with Node.js
implementation.version_scope: CoffeeScript 2; browser compatibility depends on the JavaScript emitted and any additional transpilation.

sources.label: CoffeeScript language, Node installation and compiler CLI
CoffeeScript MIT licence

fit.text: Write applications using existing JavaScript libraries while expressing the source in CoffeeScript syntax.

prerequisites.text: Install Node.js and the project-local coffeescript package; learn indentation, function arrows and the generated JavaScript.

execution.text: The compiler emits JavaScript; coffee can also compile and execute a source through Node.js.

behavior.text: CoffeeScript 2 emits modern JavaScript constructs, so the target runtime's feature support matters.

tooling.text: The CLI supports a REPL, watch mode and source maps; --transpile adds a separately installed Babel stage.

maintenance.text: Track the compiler as a local project dependency; the documentation lists changes when migrating from CoffeeScript 1.

costs.text: The compiler has MIT terms; Node.js, Babel and imported JavaScript packages remain separate components.

example.run_instructions: In a project with Node.js, install the coffeescript development dependency and run npx coffee sum.coffee. Alternatively compile with npx coffee --compile sum.coffee and run node sum.js.

implementation.name: Steel Bank Common Lisp (SBCL)

sources.label: SBCL interactive compiler, debugger and supported systems
SBCL REPL, script and saved-image behavior
SBCL ANSI conformance, extensions and FFI
SBCL public-domain and component redistribution terms

fit.text: Run ANSI Common Lisp programs in an interactive compiled environment with additional implementation facilities.

prerequisites.text: Install a supported SBCL build and learn Lisp forms through its REPL; --script provides a small file-based entry.

execution.text: SBCL evaluates interactive expressions or runs a script; applications can also be distributed as saved runtime images.

behavior.text: Standard Common Lisp semantics and SBCL extensions are separate; foreign interfaces and system-definition tools extend the implementation.

tooling.text: The implementation includes a debugger, statistical profiler and coverage tool.

maintenance.text: Saved core images have strict runtime compatibility requirements; rebuild images when changing the runtime.

costs.text: COPYING describes public-domain contributions, a jurisdictional FreeBSD fallback and separately licensed portions; retain their required notices.

example.run_instructions: With SBCL installed, run sbcl --script hello.lisp.

licenses.scope: Named implementation only; dependencies and generated applications require separate review.
licenses.notice: SBCL's COPYING describes mixed public-domain, fallback and component terms; no single SPDX expression was established for the whole distribution.

prerequisites.text: Install the compiler and learn static typing with inference rather than assuming Ruby runtime behavior.

example.run_instructions: With a Crystal compiler matching the referenced manual, run crystal run hello.cr, or crystal build hello.cr and launch the generated executable.

implementation.name: NVIDIA CUDA C++ Toolkit with nvcc
implementation.version_scope: CUDA C++ and the CUDA Runtime API; toolkit, host compiler, GPU and driver compatibility form the execution environment.

sources.label: NVIDIA CUDA C++ kernels, memory and compilation
NVIDIA CUDA Runtime device enumeration and errors
NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit EULA and supplement

fit.text: Express GPU computation through C++ kernels launched by host code; data must be available in GPU-accessible memory.

prerequisites.text: Install the CUDA Toolkit, a compatible driver and supported NVIDIA GPU; learn host/device code and thread-grid indexing.

execution.text: nvcc coordinates compilation stages; host code launches kernels with an execution configuration.

behavior.text: Many GPU threads execute a kernel; indexing and bounds checks determine each thread's valid memory accesses.

tooling.text: The Toolkit provides build, debugging and optimization tools; Nsight integrates profiling/debugging with the development workflow.

maintenance.text: Device enumeration can report initialization, insufficient-driver or no-device errors; treat compatibility checks as part of setup.

costs.text: Use and redistribution are governed by NVIDIA's SDK agreement and CUDA supplement; hardware and optional services are separate acquisitions.

example.run_instructions: With a compatible CUDA Toolkit and host C++ compiler installed, run nvcc devices.cu -o devices and launch the executable. This entry example probes device availability before developing a kernel.
example.expected_result: On a working runtime, it prints the available CUDA device count. Initialization/driver errors produce a numeric diagnostic and nonzero exit status.

implementation.name: PAKCS Curry-to-Prolog system
implementation.version_scope: PAKCS 3.x; the retrieved manual documents 3.10.0 and implementation restrictions relative to the Curry Report.

sources.label: PAKCS applications, Prolog compilation and packages
PAKCS loading, evaluation, backtracking and IO
PAKCS Prolog/Stack prerequisites and encoding
PAKCS BSD-style redistribution terms

fit.text: Model declarative computations with functional and logic programming; PAKCS documents database, web and analysis applications.

prerequisites.text: Use a supported Prolog backend; source builds also need Haskell Stack. Configure UTF-8 source encoding.

execution.text: PAKCS translates Curry to Prolog, loads a module and evaluates expressions interactively or through batch directives.

behavior.text: Nondeterministic results are enumerated through backtracking; IO actions and pure expressions have different roles.

tooling.text: CPM supplies additional libraries and tools such as analysis, documentation and property testing.

maintenance.text: The manual lists implementation restrictions against the Curry Report; verify language extensions against the selected PAKCS version.

costs.text: PAKCS has BSD three-clause terms; the selected Prolog backend and additional packages have independent licensing.

example.code:
module Reader where
main :: IO ()
main = putStrLn "PLLDN"
example.run_instructions: With PAKCS and its Prolog backend installed, run pakcs :load Reader.curry :eval main :quit from the source directory.
example.expected_result: The IO action prints PLLDN, then the batch session exits.

implementation.name: Neo4j Community Cypher engine with Cypher Shell
implementation.version_scope: Neo4j Community 2026.09 source and the current Cypher 25 manual; older databases may use Cypher 5.

sources.label: Neo4j Cypher scope and version selection
Cypher UNWIND list-to-row clause
Cypher sums, null values and grouping
Cypher Shell connections, files and fail-fast behavior
Neo4j Community GPL licence
Neo4j Community component GPL version grant

fit.text: Query property graphs declaratively; Neo4j's database engine supplies the execution environment.

prerequisites.text: Install/connect to a Neo4j development database and learn Cypher clauses, graph patterns and result rows.

execution.text: Cypher Shell sends queries through Bolt, either interactively or from a source file.

behavior.text: Aggregations collect values into groups; sum ignores null values and can return integers, floats or durations.

tooling.text: The shell supports explicit connection/database parameters, file execution and fail-fast error handling.

maintenance.text: Cypher 25 receives new features while Cypher 5 is frozen; confirm the database's configured query language.

costs.text: The named Community component permits GPL-3.0-or-later; this does not establish the licensing of other database editions or services.

example.code:
UNWIND [2, 4, 6] AS amount
RETURN sum(amount) AS total;
example.run_instructions: Connect Cypher Shell to your development Neo4j database using its documented address/user options, then execute this query interactively or pass total.cypher with -f. Authenticate through the documented interactive prompt rather than placing a password in a shared example.
example.expected_result: The query returns one row with a total column containing 12; it does not create or modify graph records.
